summary: Describes an architecture for providing integrated services over low-bitrate links such as modems, ISDN B-channels and sub-T1 links. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan for reserving a quick lane even on small, slow connections.

questions: how to reduce delay on slow links
subtitle: Making quality-of-service work on slow connections like modems.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications need consistent quality on slow links like modems, but normal packet sizes cause multi-second delays that make voice calls unusable.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture combines three techniques: real-time encapsulation to pause sending large packets and let urgent data through, header compression to shrink protocol overhead, and negotiation protocols so endpoints agree on how to compress.
tldr.outcome: Real-time flows can now work on low-speed links, though header compression cannot be deployed without consent from all endpoints on the path.

today: RFC 2689 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes an architecture for which companion implementation RFCs (2686, 2687, 2509) and header compression schemes (RFC 2508) were standardized to help real-time applications work on low-bitrate links.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Integrated services, defined in standards like RSVP, allow applications to reserve capacity on network links so that real-time traffic like voice and video gets the quality it needs. However, these standards were designed for higher-speed networks. On slow links like 28.8 kbit/s modems, 64 kbit/s ISDN, or sub-T1 links, the protocol overhead and frame sizes cause unacceptable delays.

A 1500-byte packet on a 28.8 kbit/s link ties up the link for about 400 milliseconds. A real-time voice packet arriving during this transmission must wait 400 ms—making round-trip delays over a second, which sounds like a conversation with a long echo or lag.
sections.plainLanguage: On a slow link, sending a big packet is like a large truck driving slowly down a small road. If something urgent comes along, it has to wait for the truck to finish.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The architecture targets two main goals. First, minimize end-to-end delay—especially the worst-case delay that an application must account for when planning when to play back audio. Second, maximize the bandwidth available to actual data by reducing protocol overhead.

A third concern is admission control: when a system reserves resources for a real-time flow on a low-bitrate link, it must know how much the link will actually consume after compression. Header compression and encapsulation both affect that number, so the system needs information about the stream to make a good decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep delays short so voice doesn't sound choppy. Leave more room for actual voice or video by shrinking the envelope. And be honest about how much bandwidth you really need after squeezing it down.

sections.title: Real-Time Encapsulation and Link-Layer Framing
sections.content:
The core solution is a real-time encapsulation format that allows a sender to suspend a large packet mid-stream, let a real-time packet transmit, and then resume the large packet. This is called segmentation or suspend/resume.

Two sender types emerge. Type 1 senders (like PCs) have control over each byte and naturally use the suspend/resume approach. Type 2 senders (like routers with queuing hardware) cannot suspend a frame once it leaves the queue and instead fragment all packets to a small size up front.

The RFC spec identifies two real-time encapsulation formats. One, defined in RFC 2686, extends the PPP Multilink Protocol with multiple priority classes. The other, defined in RFC 2687, uses HDLC frame delimiters to dynamically mark where one packet ends and another starts, enabling true suspend/resume without wasting overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: The trick is stopping the big truck mid-trip to let the ambulance through. Different types of hardware handle this differently: some can pause anything, others pre-cut packages into small pieces to make pausing easy.

sections.title: Header Compression for Real-Time Flows
sections.content:
Even with segmentation, the protocol stack overhead (HDLC, PPP, IP, UDP, RTP) totals 44 bytes per packet. A voice frame like G.723.1 is only 20 bytes, so the header drowns the payload.

IP header compression, designed for IPv6, cuts the 28-byte IPv4/UDP header to about 6 bytes by storing a full header once, then sending only the changing parts (sequence number, timestamp) as deltas. RTP header compression adds further techniques: differential encoding lets the sender omit the sequence number and timestamp when they follow a predictable pattern.

With both techniques, the total header can shrink to 2 bytes in favorable cases, making voice frames viable on very slow links. The compression works only between two endpoints on a link that have negotiated the scheme; the RFC emphasizes that compression requires negotiation and cannot be deployed unilaterally on an end-to-end path.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing the full address every time, write it once, then next time just say how it changed. That makes the envelope tiny.

sections.title: Negotiation and Announcement Protocols
sections.content:
For compression to work well, endpoints need to know about each real-time flow. Applications using RSVP already announce flow details in PATH messages. The RFC proposes adding new RSVP objects that describe the payload format and characteristics, which routers and hosts can use to decide which flows to compress and how.

For negotiation between peers on a link, PPP (already ubiquitous on low-bitrate links) provides a suite of protocols at link setup time. New LCP options defined in the companion RFCs (2686, 2687, 2509) let peers agree on which encapsulation format to use, which flows to compress, and how the compressor should encode the header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Before they start sending, the two endpoints talk: 'I'm sending voice, 20 bytes per packet, every 50 milliseconds.' The other side says, 'OK, I can compress that down to 2 bytes of header.'

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Header compression assumes certain application semantics. If a compressor is triggered by heuristics—for example, assuming UDP/RTP—it could misidentify traffic and decompress packets incorrectly, breaking other applications.

Hop-by-hop header compression does not work on encrypted streams because the compressor cannot observe the changing fields inside the encrypted data. If security policy allows, traffic can be decrypted at a network access server, compressed, and re-encrypted; alternatively, a special RTP payload format that encrypts only the data (not headers) can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: If you compress the wrong thing, you might break it. And you cannot squeeze down a locked package, so encryption and compression do not mix well.
